title: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
summary: Why concurrent tests pass while code is wrong, how loom systematically explores schedules and C11 memory behaviors, how ThreadSanitizer detects data races with vector clocks, and how to use both.
outcomes: Explain why stress tests miss interleaving and weak-memory bugs, and compute interleaving counts for small tests
Describe how loom replays a test under controlled schedules, with reduction and a preemption bound
Predict which store-buffering and UnsafeCell outcomes loom explores, and name loom's known model gaps
Trace ThreadSanitizer's vector clock check on a small example and explain why it reports races that did not fail
Choose between loom and TSan for a component and configure each with the right flags

lessons.title: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong

blocks.md: From the memory ordering course you know that atomics come with orderings like `Acquire` and `Release`, and from the locking course you know how a mutex turns a critical section into one indivisible step. This course is about the other half of the job: **proving to yourself that the code is actually right**, using two tools. *loom* is a Rust library that runs a test under every relevant thread schedule. *ThreadSanitizer* (TSan) is a compiler plus runtime that watches a real run and reports data races.

Start with a bug that every atomic beginner writes. Two threads each read a shared counter, then write back the value plus one. Every single access is atomic, so there is no data race in the language sense. Yet the read and the write are two separate steps, and another thread can sneak in between them.

blocks.caption: The README example of loom, written here against std. Each thread does a load (L) then a store (S).

blocks.prompt: You run this test 10,000 times on your laptop. Each run, the two threads do 2 steps each, so there are 6 possible orders of the 4 steps. In how many of those 6 orders does the assertion fail, and how often do you expect to see it fail in practice?
blocks.reveal: Enumerating all 6 orders with a script: **4 of 6 fail**. Only the two fully serial orders (L1 S1 L2 S2 and L2 S2 L1 S1) end at 2; any order where both loads happen before both stores ends at 1. Yet in practice the test usually passes, because spawning a thread takes far longer than two atomic instructions, so the first thread usually finishes before the second even starts. Failing orders are common in the space of schedules but rare in the schedules a real machine actually picks.

blocks.title: Same code, two schedules, two answers

scenes.caption: Serial schedule L1 S1 L2 S2: thread 1 reads 0 and writes 1, then thread 2 reads 1 and writes 2. The assertion holds. This is what the OS usually gives you.
Schedule L1 L2 S1 S2: both threads read 0 before either writes, so both write 1. One increment is lost and the assertion fails. Every single access was atomic.
The window that matters is the gap between L1 and S1. A failing run needs thread 2's load to land inside it. On real hardware that gap is a few instructions wide, so most runs miss it.

blocks.md: An atomic load followed by an atomic store is **not** an atomic read-modify-write. The fix here is `num.fetch_add(1, AcqRel)`, which makes L and S one indivisible step. Atomics remove data races; they do not remove race conditions in your logic.

Why not just run the test in a loop? Model it. Suppose a given run hits the bad window with probability $p$, independently each time. After $N$ runs, the chance you have seen the bug at least once is $1-(1-p)^N$. With $p = 10^{-6}$ a script gives about 1% after 10,000 runs, 63% after a million runs, and you need about 3 million runs to reach 95%.

blocks.caption: A simplified model: real runs are not independent, and p depends on the machine, the load and the compiler, which is exactly why you cannot rely on it.

blocks.title: How many stress runs until the bug shows up?

scenes.caption: With p = 1e-6, 10,000 runs see the bug only about 1% of the time. A green CI run tells you almost nothing.
Make the bug ten times rarer (p = 1e-7) and the curve slides a decade to the right. A tiny change in timing, like a faster CPU, can do this.

Rarer still (p = 1e-8) and even 100 million runs only reach about 63%. Worse, some bugs have p = 0 on your hardware: a weak-ordering bug that needs Arm reordering never appears on x86, however many runs.

blocks.md:
The loom documentation spells out the last point: when orderings weaker than `SeqCst` are involved, a bug may only occur on hardware with particular memory characteristics, so **no** amount of iteration on other hardware will show it. That is the motivation for both tools in this course:

- **loom** stops relying on luck. It takes control of the scheduler and the memory model and systematically walks through the possible executions of a small test.
- **ThreadSanitizer** stops relying on the bug *crashing*. It watches one ordinary run and flags any two conflicting accesses that are not ordered by synchronization, even if this run happened to produce the right answer.

A concurrent test that passes tells you only that the schedules your machine happened to pick were fine. To learn anything about the others you must either enumerate schedules (loom) or check the ordering rules on the schedule you got (TSan).

blocks.question: Your lock-free queue test passed 50,000 times on an x86 laptop. A teammate says it is now safe to ship to Arm servers. What is the strongest objection?
options: 50,000 runs is too few; 5 million runs would be enough
x86 hardware keeps more orderings than Arm, so a missing Release or Acquire may simply be invisible there and still break on Arm
The test should have been run in debug mode instead of release mode
Lock-free code cannot be tested at all, only proven
blocks.explain: Running more often only samples more schedules of the same hardware memory model. Weak-ordering bugs that x86's stronger hardware ordering hides have probability zero there, so no count of x86 runs covers them. A tool that models the language memory model, like loom, can explore those executions.

blocks.question: In the two-thread load-then-store counter, which change makes every schedule end at 2?
options: Use `SeqCst` for both the load and the store
Add a `thread::sleep` between the load and the store
Replace the load and store with a single `fetch_add(1, AcqRel)`
Spawn the second thread only after the first has been spawned
blocks.explain: The bug is that read and write are two steps. Stronger orderings still let another thread run between them, and sleeping only makes that more likely. `fetch_add` is one atomic read-modify-write, so no thread can observe or write between the read and the write.

lessons.title: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule

blocks.md: loom's documentation describes the idea in one line: it runs a test many times, permuting the possible concurrent executions according to the C11 memory model, and uses state reduction to avoid combinatorial explosion. To do that, loom must see every operation that can be affected by another thread. So you swap `std` types for loom's copies: `loom::sync::atomic::*`, `loom::sync::{Arc, Mutex, RwLock, Condvar}`, `loom::thread::spawn` and `loom::cell::UnsafeCell`.

The usual pattern is a crate-private `sync` module that re-exports loom types when compiled with `--cfg loom` and `std` types otherwise. Your library code imports from that module and never knows which one it got. Loom tests are run separately with `RUSTFLAGS="--cfg loom"`, and in `--release` because loom runs the closure a very large number of times.

blocks.caption: The cfg(loom) pattern from the loom docs. Only operations on loom types are visible to loom; a std Arc or Mutex hidden inside still works but is not explored.

blocks.md: Inside `loom::model(closure)` every loom operation (a load, a store, a lock, a spawn) is a **scheduling point**: loom's own scheduler, not the OS, decides which thread runs next. Loom runs the closure from start to finish, records the choices it made, then reruns it with the last undecided choice flipped, depth first, until every alternative has been tried. Because everything is replayed deterministically, a failing schedule can be saved and replayed exactly.

blocks.title: loom replaying the counter test under different schedules

scenes.caption: Execution 1. loom runs thread 1 to completion first: L1 reads 0, S1 writes 1, then thread 2 reads 1 and writes 2. The assertion passes.
Execution 2. loom backtracks to the latest choice it has not tried and switches threads right after L1. Now L2 also reads 0.
Both stores write 1. The assertion on line 12 panics, and loom reports the test as failed together with the schedule that produced it.
scenes.output:
panicked: assertion `left == right` failed
  left: 2
 right: 1

scenes.caption: Simplified: spawn and join are also scheduling points, and loom's reduction skips orders that cannot change the outcome, so the real count differs. The 6 orders of the 4 steps give 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2.

blocks.title: All 6 orders of L1, S1, L2, S2 (script-enumerated)

scenes.caption: Each column is one schedule: 1212 means thread 1, then 2, then 1, then 2, so L1 L2 S1 S2. Each thread keeps its own order. A stress test samples these with a heavily skewed distribution; loom visits them all.
Only the two serial orders give 2. These are exactly the schedules with zero preemptions, which is what an idle machine mostly produces.

Orders 1212 and 2112 differ only in the order of the two loads, which do not conflict, so loom's reduction can treat them as one; likewise 1221 and 2121. The order of the two stores still matters, since two stores conflict.

blocks.md: How many schedules are there in general? If thread $i$ performs $k_i$ visible operations, the number of interleavings that respect each thread's program order is the multinomial coefficient below. A script gives 6 for two threads with 2 steps, 20 for two threads with 3 steps, 1,680 for three threads with 3 steps, and about 5.55 trillion for three threads with 10 steps each.

blocks.caption: Counts only orderings of visible operations; real tests multiply this by data-dependent branches.

blocks.title: Interleavings explode with threads and steps

scenes.caption: Bar height is log10 of the interleaving count: 6, 20, 1,680, 184,756, about 11.7 billion and about 5.55 trillion. Each extra thread multiplies the count, which is why loom tests stay tiny.

blocks.md: loom fights this explosion with **state reduction** taken from the CDSChecker paper by Norris and Demsky, which builds on dynamic partial order reduction (DPOR). DPOR only explores a second order for two operations when they *conflict*: two stores to the same location conflict, two loads do not. The loom docs give the plain example: if two threads read the same atomic, loom does not try the other order, because it cannot change the execution.

loom only sees what goes through loom types. A `std::sync::Mutex` or a third-party lock inside your code still runs, but loom cannot schedule around it, so executions that are possible in reality are silently not modeled. Libraries you depend on need loom support too for full coverage.
Every source of non-determinism must come from loom: no real time, randomness or I/O inside `loom::model`. Determinism is what lets loom replay a schedule and flip one choice at a time.

blocks.question: In a loom test, thread A does `x.load(Acquire)` and thread B does `x.load(Acquire)` on the same atomic, with nothing else in between. How many orders of these two loads must loom explore?
options: One: two loads of the same location do not conflict, so both orders behave the same
Two: A then B, and B then A
Zero: loads are never scheduling points
It depends on LOOM_MAX_PREEMPTIONS
blocks.explain: Reordering two reads of the same location cannot change what either one returns, so the second order is equivalent and loom skips it. A load and a store, or two stores, do conflict and both orders are explored.

blocks.question: Your crate uses `parking_lot::Mutex` internally, and your loom test only swaps the atomics for loom types. What happens?
options: loom refuses to compile the test
loom explores the mutex too, because it intercepts all OS locking
The test runs, but loom cannot interleave around the lock, so some real schedules are never checked
The test always deadlocks
blocks.explain: The loom docs say interception is not automatic: concurrent operations hidden from loom still execute, but loom cannot reason about how they interact with other operations, so certain real executions are not modeled. Route the lock through your cfg(loom) sync module.

lessons.title: Preemption bounds, weak memory and what loom cannot see

blocks.md: Exhaustive search is loom's default, and for anything beyond a few operations it can run for hours. The loom docs offer a pragmatic cut: a **preemption bound**. A *preemption* is a switch where the running thread could have continued but loom forcibly stops it and runs another. With a bound of $n$, loom checks every execution that contains at most $n$ preemptions. Switches that happen because a thread blocked or finished are free.

blocks.caption: Both forms come from the loom docs and source. The docs say a bound of 2 or 3 is enough to catch most bugs in practice.

blocks.prompt: For the two-thread counter (2 steps each), how many of the 6 orders survive a preemption bound of 0, and does that bound catch the lost update?
blocks.reveal: With bound 0 a thread can only lose the CPU by finishing, so only the 2 serial orders remain, and both end at 2. **Bound 0 misses the bug.** Bound 1 allows a single forced switch, for example right after L1, which gives L1 L2 S2 S1: a failing order. A script confirms the failing orders need 1 or 2 preemptions, so any bound of at least 1 catches it.

blocks.title: Schedules checked under a preemption bound (3 threads x 3 steps)

scenes.caption: Simplified model, counted by script: 3 threads, 3 visible steps each, 1,680 interleavings in total. Bound 0 leaves just the 6 serial orders.
Each extra preemption admits many more schedules: 42 with bound 1, 192 with bound 2, 552 with bound 3.
Bound 3 covers about a third of the space (552 of 1,680); the full space needs bound 6. The bet behind bounding is that most real bugs need only a few badly timed switches.

blocks.md: Other knobs live on the same `Builder` and environment variables: `LOOM_MAX_BRANCHES` caps thread switches per execution (default 1,000 in the source), `LOOM_MAX_PERMUTATIONS` and `LOOM_MAX_DURATION` cap total work, and loom models at most `MAX_THREADS` threads, which is 5 in the current source.

Schedules are only half of it. Under the C11 memory model a load may return an **older** store, not just the latest one. Following CDSChecker, loom computes a *may-read-from* set for each load: stores to that location that are not hidden by a later store already ordered before the load by happens-before. Each choice from that set becomes another branch to explore. This is how loom finds bugs that no interleaving of instructions can produce.

blocks.caption: The store-buffering litmus test from loom's test suite (lightly condensed). Each thread stores 1 to one variable and then loads the other.

blocks.title: Store buffering: outcomes (a, b) by model

scenes.caption: All 6 interleavings of the 4 operations, run as a sequentially consistent machine (script): (1,1) four times, (0,1) once, (1,0) once. (0,0) is impossible, since some store must come first.

With Relaxed, neither load is ordered after the other thread's store, so each may read the initial 0. loom explores that and its test asserts (0,0) is observed. The new bar only marks that (0,0) is reachable; it is not an interleaving count.

blocks.md: loom also checks plain memory. Wrap non-atomic shared data in `loom::cell::UnsafeCell` and access it through `with` and `with_mut`. loom tracks causality for each access and panics with *Causality violation: Concurrent read and write accesses* when a read and a write are not ordered by happens-before. This is the loom version of a data race check, and it is exactly how a missing Release/Acquire pair on a flag shows up.

blocks.caption: From loom's UnsafeCell tests. With the guard check, reading data happens only after an Acquire load that saw the Release store, so the accesses are ordered. Without it, loom reports a causality violation.

blocks.md: Known gaps, from the loom README: `SeqCst` loads and stores are treated as `AcqRel`, which is weaker, so loom can raise **false alarms** on code that relies on SeqCst (`fence(SeqCst)` is supported). And loom does not explore **load buffering**, where a later store becomes visible to an earlier load, so it can **miss bugs**. loom is neither fully sound nor fully complete for C11.

loom's scheduler is deliberately unfair: it may never run the thread a spin loop is waiting for. Put `loom::thread::yield_now()` inside spin and retry loops so loom knows another thread must run for this one to make progress.

blocks.question: A loom test with `LOOM_MAX_PREEMPTIONS=2` passes. What can you conclude?
options: The code is correct for every schedule
The code is correct on x86 but maybe not on Arm
No execution with at most 2 forced switches violates the test's assertions, within loom's memory-model coverage
Nothing, since bounded runs are random samples
blocks.explain: A bounded run is still systematic, not random, but it only covers executions with at most 2 preemptions. It also inherits loom's model gaps (SeqCst as AcqRel, no load buffering), so it is strong evidence, not a proof.

blocks.question: A loom test of a seqlock (a lock where readers retry if a writer bumped a sequence counter) that uses `store(.., SeqCst)` panics, but you are confident the algorithm is correct under C11. What is the most likely explanation?
options: loom found a real bug that hardware hides
The preemption bound was set too high
loom does not support SeqCst at all and always panics
loom treats SeqCst loads and stores as AcqRel, so it may explore executions that SeqCst forbids, producing a false alarm
blocks.explain: The README lists this exact limitation. Check whether the failing execution relies on a reordering SeqCst would forbid; fence(SeqCst) is modeled correctly, plain SeqCst accesses are weakened.

lessons.title: ThreadSanitizer: catching races with vector clocks at runtime

blocks.md: ThreadSanitizer takes the opposite approach to loom. It does not choose schedules; it watches **one real run** of your whole program and reports every *data race* in it. A data race, as the TSan manual defines it, is two threads accessing the same variable concurrently with at least one write. C++11 makes data races undefined behavior, and so does Rust for its unsafe code.

TSan has two parts: a compiler pass and a runtime library. The compiler pass prepends every memory access that might race with a call such as `__tsan_read4(addr)` or `__tsan_write4(addr)`, skipping accesses it can prove are race-free (like reads of constant globals or locals that never escape). Atomic operations go through `__tsan_atomic` callbacks, and the runtime intercepts `pthread_mutex_lock`, `pthread_create` and friends, so it sees every synchronization event.

blocks.caption: Based on the TSan algorithm page. You never write these calls; the compiler inserts them.

blocks.md: "Concurrently" does not mean "at the same instant". TSan uses the **happens-before** relation you met in the memory ordering course: A happens before B if they are in one thread in program order, or if a release-type event (unlock, Release store, thread create) is followed by a matching acquire-type event (lock, Acquire load, join) that links them. Two conflicting accesses race if **neither happens before the other**, no matter how far apart in time they actually ran.

To decide happens-before quickly, the runtime keeps a **vector clock** per thread: one counter per thread, recording how far this thread knows each other thread has progressed. Each sync object (a mutex, an atomic) keeps a vector clock too. On a release, the object's clock takes the thread's clock; on an acquire, the thread's clock becomes the element-wise maximum of both. An earlier access by thread $u$ at time $c$ happens before the current access by thread $t$ exactly when $c \le VC_t[u]$.

blocks.title: Vector clocks with a mutex (simplified model, computed by script)

scenes.caption: Start. Each thread's own entry is 1 and it knows nothing about the other: T0 = [1,0], T1 = [0,1]. Columns are the entries for T0 and T1.
T0 (holding m) writes x. TSan records who wrote and when: T0 at time 1. Then T0's own counter ticks to 2.
T0 unlocks m, a release: the mutex copies T0's clock, m = [2,0]. T0 ticks to 3.
T1 locks m, an acquire: T1 = max([0,1],[2,0]) = [2,1]. T1 now knows about everything T0 did up to time 2.
T1 writes x. Check the old access T0@1: is 1 <= T1[T0] = 2? Yes, so it happens before. No race, and T1@1 is recorded.
Remove the lock and unlock and replay: T1 still has [0,1] when it writes x. Is 1 <= T1[T0] = 0? No, so the two writes are unordered and TSan reports a data race, even if T1 ran a full second later.

blocks.md: Where are those `T0@1` records kept? In **shadow memory**: a region whose address is computed from the application address by a fixed formula, where each 8-byte word of your memory has its own shadow cell, so finding it needs no lookup table. In the current LLVM source a shadow cell holds 4 values of 32 bits each. Each value packs an 8-bit mask of which bytes were touched, an 8-bit thread slot, a 14-bit epoch, and read and atomic flags. 4 values of 4 bytes per 8 bytes of memory makes shadow 2 times the size of the memory it covers.

blocks.title: One shadow cell per 8 bytes of application memory

scenes.caption: Two 4-byte ints x and y share one 8-byte word, so they share one shadow cell with 4 slots for recent accesses.
T1 writes x: one slot records a write of bytes 0 to 3 by T1. T2 then writes y (bytes 4 to 7). The byte masks do not overlap, so this is no race.
T2 reads x. Masks overlap with the T1 write, one is a write, different threads: TSan checks happens-before. If unordered, it reports the race.
Only 4 slots: once they fill, a new access replaces an old one. An access evicted before its racing partner arrives is forgotten, one reason TSan can miss races.

blocks.code:
$ clang -fsanitize=thread -g -O1 tiny_race.c && ./a.out
WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race (pid=19219)
  Write of size 4 at 0x7fcf47b21bc0 by thread T1:
    #0 Thread1 tiny_race.c:4 (exe+0x00000000a360)
  Previous write of size 4 at 0x7fcf47b21bc0 by main thread:
    #0 main tiny_race.c:10 (exe+0x00000000a3b4)
  Thread T1 (running) created at:
    #0 pthread_create tsan_interceptors.cc:705 (exe+0x00000000c790)
    #1 main tiny_race.c:9 (exe+0x00000000a3a4)
blocks.caption: The race report from the Clang docs: the current access, the previous conflicting access, and where the threads were created. Build with -g to get file and line.

blocks.md: TSan reports races that **did not cause a failure** in this run. It needs only that both conflicting accesses execute and that nothing orders them by happens-before. That is its big advantage over stress testing.

TSan only sees code paths that actually run (the manual: it cannot find races in code paths that are not executed). And if, in this particular run, the two threads happened to pass through some unrelated lock in between, that lock creates a happens-before edge and hides the race. Coverage and varied workloads still matter.

blocks.question: Thread A writes a global at t = 0 ms. Thread B reads it at t = 500 ms. Nothing synchronizes them, and B reads the correct value. What does TSan report?
options: A data race, because neither access happens before the other
Nothing, because the accesses were 500 ms apart and never overlapped
A data race only if halt_on_error is set
Nothing, because the read returned the correct value
blocks.explain: TSan checks the happens-before relation, not wall-clock overlap. With no release and acquire linking A to B, A's write is not visible in B's vector clock, so the pair is reported.

blocks.question: Two threads each increment a different field of one struct, `a` at offset 0 and `b` at offset 4, with no locks. Does TSan report a race?
options: Yes, they share an 8-byte shadow cell
Yes, any unsynchronized access to the same struct is a race
No, their byte masks do not overlap, so they are different memory locations
Only if the struct is heap-allocated
blocks.explain: A data race needs the same memory location. TSan records which bytes each access touched and only compares accesses whose byte ranges overlap. (They may still suffer false sharing, a performance issue, not a correctness one.)

lessons.title: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project

blocks.md: The two tools answer different questions. loom asks "is there **any** schedule or allowed memory behavior, within these bounds, where this small test fails?" TSan asks "in **this** run of the real program, did two threads touch the same memory without ordering?" One is a model checker for a few hundred lines; the other is a race detector for a whole binary.

blocks.title: Where each tool fits in the testing pipeline

scenes.caption: Small, subtle concurrent primitives get loom tests: few threads, few operations, every schedule within the bound.
The whole program, with real libraries and real workloads, runs under a TSan build. It finds races in code paths loom never modeled.
Both run in CI as separate jobs. The shipped binary is a normal build: the Clang docs say the TSan runtime is not meant for production executables.

blocks.md: Running TSan is mostly a build flag. Compile **and** link with `-fsanitize=thread`, add `-O1` or higher for reasonable speed and `-g` for line numbers. The Clang docs list typical costs of 5 to 15 times slower and 5 to 10 times more memory; the older TSan manual says 2 to 20 times slower. TSan maps a lot of virtual address space without reserving it, so `top` can look alarming and `ulimit` may misbehave. Only 64-bit platforms are supported, and static linking of libc or libstdc++ is not.

blocks.code:
# C or C++: compile and link with -fsanitize=thread; -O1+ for speed, -g for lines
clang++ -fsanitize=thread -O1 -g app.cc -o app
TSAN_OPTIONS="halt_on_error=1 history_size=4" ./app   # exit code 66 on report

# Rust (nightly): the std library must be rebuilt with the sanitizer too
export RUSTFLAGS=-Zsanitizer=thread RUSTDOCFLAGS=-Zsanitizer=thread
cargo +nightly test -Zbuild-std --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu

# suppress a known third-party race (suppressions file)
# race:third_party::Cache::refresh
TSAN_OPTIONS="suppressions=tsan.supp" ./app
blocks.caption: Commands and flags from the Clang TSan docs and the Rust unstable book. Rust TSan needs nightly and -Zbuild-std.

blocks.md:
The runtime flags you will reach for most, all set in `TSAN_OPTIONS` and documented on the Clang page:

- `halt_on_error=1` exits after the first report (default off). TSan's exit code on a report is 66 by default, unlike other sanitizers.
- `history_size` (0 to 7, default 0) controls how much per-thread access history is kept for the *previous access* stack. Raise it when a report says *failed to restore the stack*.
- `suppressions=file` hides known races you cannot fix yet, for example in third-party code.
- `detect_deadlocks` (default on) reports a **lock-order-inversion (potential deadlock)** when two locks are taken in opposite orders on different paths, even if this run did not deadlock.
- `force_seq_cst_atomics=1` treats every atomic as SeqCst, handy for checking whether a bug comes from relaxed ordering.

TSan must see **all** synchronization. Code not built with the flag (a prebuilt library, inline assembly) can cause false positives or missed races. That is why Rust's std should be rebuilt with the sanitizer via `-Zbuild-std`. The Rust unstable book also says Rust TSan does not support `std::sync::atomic::fence` or synchronization done in inline assembly, and rebuilding std does not change that.

A practical split many Rust projects use: write loom tests for the small lock-free core where orderings are subtle, and run the full test suite and a realistic workload under TSan. The two find different bugs. loom finds the rare schedule and the weak-memory outcome on a toy-sized test. TSan finds the unsynchronized access deep in real code, but only on the path and with the synchronization that this run happened to take. For deadlocks, loom panics with a deadlock error when an explored schedule leaves every thread blocked, while TSan flags inconsistent lock order without needing the deadlock to happen.

blocks.title: Which tool catches which bug (1 = designed to catch it)

scenes.caption: Qualitative summary of this course (not measurements): 1 means the tool is designed to catch it, 0.5 partially, 0.3 only by luck. TSan reports data races, not logic races between atomic steps.
A missing Release/Acquire on a flag guarding plain data shows up in TSan as a race on that data, if both accesses run. With atomics only, TSan reports no race; loom explores the stale read.
loom weakens SeqCst to AcqRel, so code that needs SeqCst can give false alarms there. Neither tool helps on code no test executes: coverage is still your job.

blocks.md: Use loom to search **schedules** of a tiny test exhaustively, and TSan to check **ordering** on real runs of the whole program. Neither proves correctness alone; together they cover far more than any number of stress runs.

blocks.question: A CI job runs your C++ service's integration tests under `-fsanitize=thread` and reports nothing for months. Which statement is justified?
options: The service is free of data races
TSan is misconfigured, since every large program has races
The service cannot deadlock
No data race occurred, unordered by happens-before, on the code paths and synchronization these tests exercised
blocks.explain: TSan is a dynamic detector: it is precise about what it saw but blind to paths that never ran and to races hidden by incidental synchronization in this run. Clean reports are evidence about the executed paths only.

blocks.question: You maintain a lock-free single-producer single-consumer ring buffer in Rust (about 80 lines) and a large async web service that uses it. Where should each tool go?
options: TSan on the ring buffer, loom on the web service
loom on the ring buffer with 2 threads and a small capacity; TSan on the service's test suite
loom on both, with LOOM_MAX_PREEMPTIONS=0 to keep it fast
Neither: Rust's borrow checker already rules out data races
blocks.explain: loom shines on small primitives with subtle orderings, and its cost explodes with threads and steps, so keep the model tiny. The service has far too many operations for loom but runs fine under TSan. Bound 0 would only check serial schedules, and the borrow checker does not check unsafe code or atomic orderings.

blocks.question: A TSan report shows the current stack but says *failed to restore the stack* for the previous access. What do you change?
